qt: to the Commission Grégory Allione (Renew) Subject:

Recently, Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk firefighting helicopters were deployed under the rescEU mechanism to fight a fire in the Drôme department of France. However, those helicopters are US-designed military aircraft and are not covered by the civil certification scheme of the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), which applies to comparable European aircraft. This raises questions about the consistency of EU requirements for aviation safety and fair competition. In its reply of 25 June 2026 to a previous parliamentary communication, the Commission itself pointed out that the lack of harmonisation of aircraft certification rules could lead to operational difficulties, restrictions on cross-border operations and fragmentation of the EU market. EASA certification ensures a high level of safety, continued airworthiness, operational interoperability and maintenance, while also creating a level playing field between EU manufacturers and non-EU suppliers. In light of the above: 1.
What specific initiatives does the Commission intend to implement to encourage Member States to make use of the mechanism provided for in Article 2(6) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1139?
What steps does it intend to take to strengthen the European industrial base and reduce the EU’s dependence on aerial capabilities from outside the EU to fight forest fires?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.10.2026) With regard to aircraft covered by Article 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 2018/11391, including firefighting aircraft, the Regulation fully preserves the prerogative of Member States to decide whether to make use of the mechanism provided for in Article 2(6). In this respect, the Commission’s role is limited to drawing attention to the potential advantages that such a choice may offer. At the same time, Europe’s immediate aerial firefighting needs call for a solution that can be deployed in the near term and is based on an aircraft type that is available within a short timeframe and with an established operational track record. The Commission has allocated significant financial resources for the acquisition of 12 new firefighting airplanes, hosted by several Member States, which will form the permanent rescEU fleet. European alternatives are currently under development and monitored by the Commission. These projects, if successful, could help strengthen Europe’s strategic and industrial autonomy. However, they might face the challenges inherent in designing and certifying an entirely new aircraft, with first deliveries expected only in several years’ time.
